title.en: Your first day: names, time and word order

summary.en: Introduce yourself and say that today is your first day.

body.en:
Titus opens with **Ja, ich bin Titus.** — “Yes, I’m Titus.” To introduce yourself, use *Ich bin* and your name. The verb *sein* changes unusually: *ich bin*, *du bist*, *er ist*, *wir sind*. Do not build the first-person form from the infinitive by adding a regular ending.

**Heute ist mein erster Tag hier.** means “Today is my first day here.” A German statement can begin with a time expression. The finite verb stays in the second position: *Heute ist …*. Compare *Mein erster Tag ist heute.* — “My first day is today.” A position can contain a whole phrase; it does not mean the second written word in every sentence.

*Tag* is masculine. After *mein*, the describing word carries the masculine nominative ending: **mein erster Tag**. In the original interview Titus uses a different, equally natural construction, *Ich hab heute meinen ersten Tag hier.* There the first-day phrase is the object of *haben*, so it takes the accusative: *meinen ersten Tag*. The beginner story deliberately uses the simpler *Heute ist …* version.

Finally, *hier* means “here”, the workplace in this scene. Try substituting your own name, then changing the time: *Morgen ist mein erster Tag.* — “Tomorrow is my first day.” These practice examples are new sentences, not extra dialogue attributed to the programme.
